questions.stem: Which set of conditions is needed for evolution by natural selection?
options: A stable environment in which no individual faces competition, predation or disease
Heritable variation, more offspring than can survive, and better survival of some variants
Individuals changing during their lifetime to suit the environment, then passing those changes on
A population that stays the same size, with every individual having an equal chance of survival
questions.explanation: Natural selection needs inherited variation, a struggle for survival because more offspring are produced than survive, and differences in survival and reproduction linked to the trait. Changes acquired during a lifetime are not inherited.

questions.stem: What is the original source of new genetic variation in a population?
options: Predation
Mutation
Natural selection
Competition
questions.explanation: Mutations create new alleles; meiosis and fertilisation then reshuffle them into new combinations. Natural selection acts on variation that already exists; it does not create it.

questions.stem: A kangaroo develops very strong leg muscles through years of hopping long distances. Why will its joeys not inherit stronger muscles as a result?
options: Changes acquired during a lifetime do not alter the DNA in the parent's gametes
Joeys inherit only their mother's traits, and only males hop long distances
Strong muscles are a dominant trait, so they appear only every second generation
Muscle strength is an environmental factor, so no genes are involved at all
questions.explanation: Only genetic information in gametes is passed on, and exercise does not change the alleles in sperm or eggs. This is why the idea of inheriting acquired characteristics was rejected.

questions.stem: In evolutionary terms, what does it mean for an individual to have high fitness?
options: It can change its traits to suit any environment it meets
It survives and reproduces successfully, passing on more of its alleles
It is the strongest and fastest member of the whole population it lives in
It lives for longer than any other individual of its species
questions.explanation: Fitness is measured by reproductive success: how many offspring an individual leaves, and so how much it contributes to the next generation's gene pool. A strong, long-lived individual that does not reproduce has low fitness.

questions.stem: A population of a native grass varies in drought tolerance. After several years of severe drought, most plants in the population are drought tolerant. Which explanation is correct?
options: The grass population decided to become tolerant so that the species would not become extinct
Tolerant plants survived and reproduced more, so the alleles for tolerance became more common
The drought caused the plants to mutate, producing exactly the tolerance that each of them needed
Each plant gradually became more tolerant during the drought and passed this on to its seeds
questions.explanation: The variation already existed; the drought acted as a selective pressure, so tolerant plants left more offspring and their alleles increased in frequency. Environments do not cause the mutations an organism needs, and populations do not evolve by choice.

questions.stem: The myxoma virus was released in Australia in 1950 to control rabbits. At first it killed most infected rabbits, but rabbit populations later became more resistant. What best explains this?
options: Rabbits learned to avoid the virus, and taught this behaviour to their offspring
The virus acted as a selective pressure, so rabbits with resistance survived and bred
Rabbits developed immunity during infection and passed this acquired immunity on to their young
The virus caused mutations for resistance in every rabbit that it infected
questions.explanation: Rabbits with inherited resistance were more likely to survive and reproduce, so resistance alleles became more common: a human-induced selective pressure. Immunity acquired during an infection is not inherited genetically.

questions.stem: How can evolution by natural selection lead to an increase in species diversity?
options: Natural selection removes all variation from a population, so it splits into different species
Species combine with other species when they meet, producing a larger number of new species
Isolated populations meet different selective pressures and diverge into separate species
Every individual in a species changes in the same direction until it becomes a new species
questions.explanation: When populations are isolated, different environments select for different traits and they accumulate different mutations. Over time they may become unable to interbreed, forming new species.

questions.stem: Kangaroos, wombats, koalas and possums are thought to have evolved from a common marsupial ancestor, each adapted to a different way of life. What is this an example of?
options: Divergent evolution (adaptive radiation)
Convergent evolution (analogous change)
Punctuated equilibrium (rapid bursts)
Artificial selection (selective breeding)
questions.explanation: A single ancestral group diversifying into many forms suited to different niches is divergent evolution, or adaptive radiation. Convergent evolution is the opposite pattern: unrelated groups becoming similar.

questions.stem: Which animal was part of Australia's extinct megafauna?
options: Bilby
Quokka
Diprotodon
Brushtail possum
questions.explanation: Diprotodon was a giant herbivorous marsupial, the largest marsupial known, and one of many very large animals known from Australian fossils. Brushtail possums, bilbies and quokkas are living, much smaller marsupials.

questions.stem: Which features are shared by all monotremes, such as the platypus and echidnas?
options: They give birth to live young nourished by a placenta
They lay eggs and feed their young on milk
They give birth to live young that develop in a pouch
They lay eggs and have feathers to keep warm
questions.explanation: Monotremes are egg-laying mammals; like all mammals they produce milk, although they have no nipples. Marsupials give birth to live young that usually complete development in a pouch.

questions.stem: Why did marsupials diversify into so many forms in Australia?
options: Australia was joined to Asia, so marsupials could move in freely from many different continents
Marsupials evolved only in Australia, so no other continent has ever had marsupials
Marsupials can change their body shape during life to fill any niche that becomes free
Australia was isolated for a long time, with few placental mammals to compete with marsupials
questions.explanation: After Australia separated from the rest of Gondwana, marsupials evolved in isolation and radiated into many niches filled by placental mammals elsewhere. Marsupials also live in the Americas, so they did not evolve only in Australia.

questions.stem: A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed. Which adaptation lets it find prey?
options: A long sticky tongue that it flicks out to catch prey by touch
Echolocation clicks that bounce off prey and return to its ears
Receptors in its bill that detect weak electric fields from prey
Large eyes with many rod cells that see clearly in murky water
questions.explanation: The platypus bill has electroreceptors and touch receptors that detect the tiny electrical signals and movements of prey such as insect larvae. Its eyes and ears are closed while diving.

questions.stem: Living marsupials are found in Australia and the Americas, and fossil marsupials have been found in Antarctica. What does this distribution best support?
options: The continents were once joined in Gondwana, and marsupials spread across it before it broke up
Marsupials evolved separately on each continent from different ancestors that were not marsupials
Marsupials swam between the continents across open ocean after the continents had separated
Marsupials were carried between continents by humans long after the continents separated
questions.explanation: Australia, Antarctica and South America were connected as part of Gondwana. Marsupials spread across this land before it broke apart, then evolved in isolation on each fragment.

questions.stem: What is convergent evolution?
options: Closely related species evolving very different features as they adapt to different environments
Two species evolving together, each acting as a selective pressure on the other
A single species staying unchanged for millions of years in a stable environment
Unrelated species evolving similar features because they face similar selective pressures
questions.explanation: In convergent evolution, similar environments or ways of life select for similar traits in organisms that are not closely related, producing analogous structures. Related species becoming different is divergent evolution.

questions.stem: The sugar glider, an Australian marsupial, and the North American flying squirrel, a placental mammal, both have a skin membrane between their limbs for gliding. What explains this similarity?
options: Convergent evolution, because similar lifestyles in trees selected for similar features
Divergent evolution, because they share a recent gliding ancestor that lived in Australia
Close relationship, because both animals are marsupials with the same ancestor
Inheritance of acquired traits, because each stretched its skin while jumping
questions.explanation: The two are only distantly related, one a marsupial and one a placental mammal, but gliding between trees selected for similar membranes in each. Their gliding membranes are analogous structures.

questions.stem: The extinct thylacine had a skull remarkably similar to a wolf's, but it carried its young in a pouch and was more closely related to other Australian marsupials. What should be concluded?
options: The skull similarity proves the thylacine and wolf share a recent ancestor, so the pouch is convergent
The thylacine evolved from wolves that reached Australia and later developed a pouch for their young
Skull shape is the best evidence of relationship, so the thylacine should be classified as a placental
The skull similarity is convergent, and does not show that the thylacine and wolf are closely related
questions.explanation: Similar predatory lifestyles selected for similar skulls in two unrelated lineages. Fundamental features such as the pouch and reproductive biology, and DNA evidence, show the thylacine was a marsupial.

questions.stem: Students scatter green and brown beads on green grass, then a 'predator' picks up as many beads as possible in 30 seconds. More green beads remain. What does the predator represent?
options: The environment changing the colours of the beads directly
A selective pressure acting on the variation in colour
A source of new variation through mutation in the beads
The inheritance of colour from one generation to the next
questions.explanation: The predator removes the more conspicuous beads, just as predation selects against poorly camouflaged prey. The model does not include mutation or inheritance unless extra steps are added.

questions.stem: Which is the most important limitation of the bead model of natural selection?
options: The beads come in different colours, which is not how variation occurs in a real population
The predator picks up some beads but not others, which never happens in real populations
The background is a single colour, which means camouflage cannot be modelled at all
The beads do not reproduce, so inheritance and change across generations must be imitated
questions.explanation: The model shows variation and selection well, but survivors do not breed, so inheritance, new mutations and changes over many generations are not truly represented. Colour variation and selective predation are exactly what the model is designed to show.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a behavioural adaptation?
options: A plant having stomata sunk into pits in its leaves
A lizard basking in the sun on a cold morning
A cactus storing water in a thick fleshy stem
A fish producing large amounts of dilute urine
questions.explanation: A behavioural adaptation is something an organism does. Water storage tissue and sunken stomata are structural adaptations, and producing dilute urine is physiological.

questions.stem: Which correctly classifies these adaptations: sunken stomata in Hakea, salt excretion from the leaves of grey mangroves, and koalas hugging cool tree trunks on hot days?
options: Physiological, structural, behavioural
Behavioural, physiological, structural
Structural, behavioural, physiological
Structural, physiological, behavioural
questions.explanation: Sunken stomata are a feature of body structure, excreting salt through leaf glands is a body process, and moving to press against cooler trunks is a behaviour.

questions.stem: Many Australian wattles (Acacia) have phyllodes: flattened leaf stalks that replace true leaves and often hang vertically. How does this help them in dry conditions?
options: The phyllodes absorb water directly from the air, so the plant needs no roots in dry soil
The phyllodes store large amounts of water, so the plant can survive without stomata
A smaller, tougher surface faces the midday sun edge-on, reducing heating and water loss
A larger, thinner surface faces the midday sun directly, increasing photosynthesis and cooling
questions.explanation: Phyllodes are tough and often held vertically, so less surface is exposed to the hot midday sun, reducing leaf temperature and transpiration. They still have stomata and rely on roots for water.

questions.stem: Leaves of spinifex grass (Triodia) are tightly rolled, with the stomata on the inner surface. How does this structure reduce water loss?
options: Humid air is trapped around the stomata, reducing the water vapour gradient to the outside air
The rolled leaf stores water in its centre, which the stomata absorb when the soil dries
The stomata face the sun, so the heat closes them permanently during the day
The rolled leaf exposes more surface to the wind, which carries water vapour back in
questions.explanation: Rolling encloses the stomata in a still, humid space, so the concentration gradient for water vapour diffusion is smaller and less water is lost. Exposing stomata to wind would increase water loss.

questions.stem: Some Banksia species have stomata in pits (crypts) on the underside of the leaf, lined with hairs. What is the main advantage?
options: Hairs and pits reflect light into the stomata, increasing the rate of photosynthesis
Hairs and pits trap still, moist air over the stomata, so transpiration is reduced
Hairs and pits increase air movement over the stomata, so more carbon dioxide enters
Hairs and pits hold rainwater, which the stomata absorb directly into the leaf
questions.explanation: Stomata in hairy crypts lie in a layer of still, humid air, which lowers the water vapour gradient and reduces water loss. Increasing air movement would speed up transpiration.

questions.stem: The grey mangrove grows in salty, waterlogged mud. Which pair of adaptations helps it survive there?
options: Leaves that absorb fresh water from the air, and roots with no need for oxygen
Pneumatophores that take in air for the roots, and salt glands that excrete salt from leaves
Deep tap roots that reach fresh groundwater below the mud, and thin leaves without any cuticle
Large air-filled leaves that float, and roots that store all excess salt permanently
questions.explanation: Waterlogged mud has little oxygen, so pencil-like roots called pneumatophores grow up into the air for gas exchange. Excess salt taken up with water is excreted through glands on the leaves.

questions.stem: Students compare cross-sections of leaves from a rainforest plant and a desert plant. Which observation indicates an adaptation to an arid environment?
options: A thin cuticle and a large number of stomata on the upper surface
Large air spaces and many stomata held above the leaf surface
Wide, thin leaf blades with stomata exposed on both surfaces
A thick waxy cuticle and stomata sunk below the leaf surface
questions.explanation: A thick cuticle reduces evaporation through the epidermis, and sunken stomata sit in humid air, reducing transpiration. Thin cuticles and many exposed stomata suit humid places where water is plentiful.

questions.stem: What is an ectotherm?
options: An animal that lives only in cold environments and cannot survive heat
An animal that produces all of its body heat by shivering its muscles
An animal whose body temperature depends mainly on heat from the environment
An animal that keeps a constant body temperature using heat from metabolism
questions.explanation: Ectotherms, such as lizards, snakes and frogs, gain most of their heat from their surroundings and regulate temperature mainly by behaviour. Using metabolic heat to stay constant describes an endotherm.

questions.stem: A bearded dragon basks in the morning sun, then moves between shade and sun during the hottest part of the day. What does this behaviour achieve?
options: It lets it make extra body heat by metabolism when it is in shade
It stops it needing to eat, because sunlight replaces its food
It keeps its body temperature within a range suitable for activity
It keeps its body temperature exactly equal to the air temperature
questions.explanation: By shuttling between sun and shade, an ectotherm can keep its body temperature in a preferred range, often well above the air temperature in the morning. Sunlight provides heat, not food energy.

questions.stem: On very hot days, koalas move lower down trees and press their bodies against the cooler trunks. What type of adaptation is this, and what does it achieve?
options: A behavioural adaptation that transfers heat from the body to the cooler trunk
A structural adaptation that increases the thickness of fur to block heat
A physiological adaptation that lowers metabolic rate to make less heat
A behavioural adaptation that helps the koala reach fresher leaves to eat
questions.explanation: Moving to a cooler surface is a behaviour; heat passes from the warmer body to the cooler trunk by conduction, so the koala needs to lose less water by panting.

questions.stem: The bilby lives in arid inland Australia. It spends the day in a deep burrow and is active at night. How does this behaviour help it survive?
options: It increases water loss, which cools its body during the night
It avoids the heat of the day, reducing water loss for cooling
It lets it absorb more heat at night when the desert is coldest
It lets it photosynthesise in the burrow while it is sheltered
questions.explanation: Burrows are cooler and more humid than the surface, and nocturnal activity avoids the hottest part of the day, so the bilby needs little water for evaporative cooling. Animals do not photosynthesise.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the body temperature of animal X stayed at about 37°C at air temperatures from 5°C to 35°C. Animal Y's body temperature was within 2°C of the air temperature throughout. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Both are endotherms, because both survived
Both are ectotherms, because both were tested
X is an endotherm and Y is an ectotherm
X is an ectotherm and Y is an endotherm
questions.explanation: A constant body temperature across a range of air temperatures shows internal regulation using metabolic heat, which is endothermy. A body temperature that tracks the environment is typical of an ectotherm without access to basking sites.

questions.stem: A bobtail lizard and a rat of similar body mass live in the same area. Why does the lizard need much less food?
options: It gets energy from sunlight by photosynthesis in its skin cells
It has a larger SA:V ratio, so it absorbs nutrients through its skin
It does not use energy from food to keep its body temperature constant
It has a higher metabolic rate, so it uses its food more efficiently
questions.explanation: Endotherms such as rats spend much of their food energy generating heat to keep warm. Ectotherms rely on environmental heat, so their metabolic rate and food needs are much lower.

questions.stem: How does a freshwater bony fish maintain its water and salt balance?
options: It stores urea in its blood so it has the same concentration as fresh water
It produces large volumes of dilute urine and actively takes up salts through its gills
It drinks large amounts of water and actively excretes salts through its gills
It produces small volumes of concentrated urine and loses salts through its skin
questions.explanation: Its body fluids are saltier than fresh water, so it constantly gains water by osmosis and loses salts. It gets rid of the water as dilute urine and replaces salts by active uptake at the gills.

questions.stem: How does a marine bony fish maintain its water and salt balance?
options: It absorbs water through its skin by active transport and stores salt in its muscles
It produces large volumes of dilute urine to remove the water that it gains by osmosis
It drinks seawater, actively excretes salt through its gills and makes little urine
It avoids drinking, takes up salt through its gills and makes large amounts of urine
questions.explanation: Its body fluids are less salty than seawater, so it loses water by osmosis. It replaces water by drinking, then uses active transport in gill cells to excrete the extra salt, producing only a small volume of urine.

questions.stem: Sharks keep high concentrations of urea in their blood. How does this help them in seawater?
options: It reacts with the salt in seawater and removes it, so they can drink seawater safely
It raises the solute concentration of body fluids close to seawater, so little water is lost by osmosis
It lowers the solute concentration of body fluids well below seawater, so water floods in by osmosis
It is converted to glucose in the blood, giving them energy to pump salt out of their gills
questions.explanation: Retaining urea makes shark body fluids about as concentrated as seawater, or slightly more, so they do not lose water by osmosis as bony marine fish do. Excess salt is removed by a rectal gland.

questions.stem: The saltwater crocodile can live in the sea for long periods. Which adaptation helps it deal with the salt it takes in?
options: Scales that absorb fresh water from the seawater
Lungs that remove salt from the air it breathes
Salt glands on its tongue that excrete excess salt
Kidneys that produce urine saltier than seawater
questions.explanation: Saltwater crocodiles have salt glands on the tongue that secrete concentrated salt solution, a physiological adaptation also found in other forms in sea turtles and seabirds. Reptile kidneys cannot make urine more concentrated than their blood.

questions.stem: What does the punctuated equilibrium model of evolution propose?
options: Slow, steady change at a constant rate over very long periods of time
Change only when organisms decide to adapt to their environment
No change at all once a species has first formed from its ancestor
Long periods of little change interrupted by short bursts of rapid change
questions.explanation: Punctuated equilibrium, proposed by Eldredge and Gould, describes long periods of stasis broken by relatively rapid change, often linked to speciation. Slow, constant change is the gradualism model.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree drawn against time, how do gradualism and punctuated equilibrium differ in appearance?
options: Gradualism shows branches that end abruptly; punctuated equilibrium shows branches that all continue to the present
Gradualism shows branches diverging slowly at angles; punctuated equilibrium shows long vertical lines with sudden sideways jumps
Gradualism shows long vertical lines with sudden sideways jumps; punctuated equilibrium shows branches diverging slowly at angles
Gradualism shows a single unbranched line; punctuated equilibrium shows many branches that rejoin each other later
questions.explanation: With time on the vertical axis, gradual change appears as slowly diverging, sloping branches. Punctuated equilibrium appears as vertical lines (stasis) with near-horizontal segments where rapid change occurs.

questions.stem: How does a population of bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic?
options: The antibiotic causes every bacterium to mutate so that it becomes resistant
The bacteria learn to avoid the antibiotic and pass this learning to new cells
The patient's body becomes used to the antibiotic, so it stops working on bacteria
A few bacteria already carry resistance alleles; they survive treatment and multiply
questions.explanation: Resistance arises by random mutation or by gaining resistance genes, before or independently of exposure. The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply. It is the bacteria, not the patient, that become resistant.

questions.stem: DDT was sprayed widely to kill mosquitoes that carry malaria. Within years, many mosquito populations were resistant. Which explanation is correct?
options: DDT entered the mosquitoes' eggs and changed their DNA, so the next generation was resistant
Mosquitoes exposed to small doses built up a tolerance, which their offspring then inherited
DDT broke down in the environment, so mosquitoes that hatched later were exposed to none of it
Mosquitoes with alleles giving resistance survived spraying and passed them on, so resistance became common
questions.explanation: DDT was a strong human-induced selective pressure: mosquitoes with resistance mutations survived and reproduced, and with short generation times resistance spread rapidly. Tolerance built up during a lifetime is not inherited.

questions.stem: Why can antibiotic resistance spread through bacterial populations much faster than most adaptations spread through animal populations?
options: Bacteria reproduce sexually every generation, so new combinations of alleles appear each time
Bacteria cannot mutate, so every resistance gene they carry is passed on without any change
Bacteria have very short generation times and can pass resistance genes to other bacteria on plasmids
Bacteria have very long generation times and can choose which genes to pass to their offspring
questions.explanation: Bacteria can divide every 20 minutes or so in good conditions, so selection acts over many generations quickly. Plasmids carrying resistance genes can also be transferred between bacteria, even between species.
